title: Boiled Leg Of Mutton
description: Prepared with garlic, carrots, and turnips.
steps: Cut off the shank, wrap the flank nicely round and secure it with skewers
Dredge it well with flour, and put it on the fire in a kettle of cold water with some salt
And three or four heads of garlic, which will give it a delicately fine flavour
Skin it well, and when nearly done, take it from the fire and keep it hot and closely covered, that the steam may finish it
Have carrots well boiled to put in the dish under it, or turnips boiled, mashed smooth and stewed with a lump of butter and salt
Lay the mutton on, and pour over it butter melted with some flour in it
And a cup full of capers with some of the vinegar
Shake them together over the fire till hot before you pour it on

title: Boiled Potatoes
description: Prepared with potatoes, water, and salt.
steps: Select potatoes that are as nearly as possible of the same size
Wash, but do not pare them
Put them into a pot with water enough to cover them about an inch, and do not put on the pot-lid
When the water is very near boiling, pour it off, and replace it with the same quantity of cold water, into which throw a good portion of salt
Potatoes of a moderate size will require about half an hour boiling; large ones an hour
Try them with a fork
When done, pour off the water, cover the pot with a folded napkin, or flannel, and let them stand by the fire about a quarter of an hour to dry
Peel them and send them to table

Put it in a saucepan, with a quart of clean water and a pinch of salt

title: Boiled Salmon (Fresh)
description: Prepared with salmon, cream or milk, and egg yolks.

ingredients.name: cream or half milk and half cream, pint
ingredients.sourceText: cream or half milk and half cream, pint

ingredients.name: water in which the fish is boiled, half-gill
ingredients.sourceText: water in which the fish is boiled, half-gill

steps: Wrap the fish, when you have washed and wiped it, in a clean linen cloth—not too thick.
Baste it up securely, and put into the fish-kettle.
Cover with cold water in which has been melted a handful of salt.
Boil slowly, allowing about a quarter of an hour to each pound.
When the time is up, rip open a corner of the cloth and test the salmon with a fork.
If it penetrate easily, it is done. If not, hastily pin up the cloth and cook a little longer.
Skim off the scum as it rises to the top.
Have ready in another saucepan a pint of cream—or half milk and half cream will do—which has been heated in a vessel set in boiling water.
Stir into this a large spoonful of butter, rolled in flour, a little salt and chopped parsley, and a half-gill of the water in which the fish is boiled.
Let it boil up once, stirring all the while.
When the fish is done, take it instantly from the kettle, lay it an instant upon a folded cloth to absorb the drippings.
Transfer with great care, for fear of breaking, to a hot dish, and pour the boiled cream over it, reserving enough to fill a small sauce-boat.
Garnish with curled parsley and circular slices of hard-boiled yolks—leaving out the whites of the eggs.

title: Boston Cream Cakes
description: A cake made with milk or cream, vanilla bean, and white sugar.

ingredients.name: a quart of rich milk or cream
ingredients.sourceText: a quart of rich milk or cream

ingredients.name: a stick of the best Ceylon cinnamon
ingredients.sourceText: a stick of the best Ceylon cinnamon

ingredients.name: a quarter of a pound or more of powdered white sugar
ingredients.sourceText: a quarter of a pound or more of powdered white sugar

ingredients.name: half a pound of fine flour
ingredients.sourceText: half a pound of fine flour

ingredients.name: half a pound of fresh butter
ingredients.sourceText: half a pound of fresh butter

steps: From a quart of rich milk or cream take half a pint, and put it into a small saucepan, with a vanilla bean, and a stick of the best Ceylon cinnamon, broken in pieces.
Cover the saucepan closely, and let it boil till the milk is highly flavoured with the vanilla and cinnamon.
Strain it, take out the vanilla bean, wipe it, and put it away.
Mix the flavoured milk with the other pint and a half, and let it get quite cold.
Beat very light the yolks only of twelve eggs, and stir them into the milk alternately with a quarter of a pound, or more, of powdered white sugar.
Put this custard mixture into a tin pan, set it in a Dutch oven or something similar, pour round the pan some boiling water, enough to reach half-way up its sides, and bake the custard ten minutes.
Sift half a pound of fine flour, cut up half a pound of fresh butter in a pint of rich milk, and set it on a stove or near the fire till the butter is soft but not melted.
Stir it well and take it off.
Beat eight whole eggs very light, and stir them gradually into the milk and butter, in turn with the flour.
Ensure the batter is very smooth and quite free from lumps.
Put the batter in equal portions into deep pattypans with plain unscolloped sides, filling them but little more than half.
Sprinkle powdered loaf-sugar over the top of each.
Set them immediately into a brisk oven, and bake them about a quarter of an hour, or twenty minutes, until well browned.
When done, take them out, and open in the side of each (while quite hot) a slit or cut, large enough to admit a portion of the custard.
Put in with a spoon as much of the custard as will amply fill the cavity or hollow in the middle of each cake.
Close the slit nicely, by pinching and smoothing it with your thumb and finger, and set the cakes to cool.
Eat fresh.

title: Boston Cream Cakes
description: A cake made with corn, vanilla or lemon, and butter.
steps: Stir the butter into the water, which should be warm, set it on the fire in a saucepan, and slowly bring to a boil, stirring it often.
When it boils, put in the flour, boil one minute, stirring all the while.
Take from the fire, turn into a deep dish, and let it cool.
Beat the eggs very light, and whip into this cooled paste, first the yolks, then the whites.
Drop, in great spoonfuls, upon buttered paper, taking care not to let them touch or run into each other, and bake ten minutes.
For the cream: Wet the corn-starch with enough milk to work it into a smooth paste.
Boil the rest of the milk.
Beat the eggs, add the sugar and corn-starch to these, and so soon as the milk boils pour in the mixture gradually, stirring all the time until smooth and thick.
Drop in a teaspoonful of butter, and when this is mixed in, set the custard aside to cool.
Add vanilla or lemon seasoning.
Pass a sharp knife lightly around the puffs, split them, and fill with the mixture.

title: Boston Pork and Beans
description: Prepared with white beans, salt pork, and salt.

ingredients.name: a quart of small, white beans
ingredients.sourceText: a quart of small, white beans

ingredients.name: soda the size of a bean
ingredients.sourceText: soda the size of a bean

steps: Pick over carefully the beans.
Let them soak over night in cold water.
In the morning wash and drain in another water.
Put on to boil in plenty of cold water with a piece of soda the size of a bean.
Let them come to a boil, then drain again, cover with water once more, and boil them fifteen minutes, or until the skin of the beans will crack when taken out and blown upon.
Drain the beans again, put them into an earthen pot, adding a tablespoonful of salt.

Cover with hot water, place in the centre a pound of salt pork, first scalding it with hot water, and scoring the rind across the top, a quarter of an inch apart to indicate where the slices are to be cut.
Place the pot in the oven, and bake six hours or longer.
Keep the oven a moderate heat.
Add hot water from the tea-kettle as needed, on account of evaporation, to keep the beans moist.
When the meat becomes crisp and looks cooked, remove it, as too long baking the pork destroys its solidity.

Wipe them and spread them on a soft table-cloth, covering them over with several folds

title: Bread
description: A bread preparation made with wheat flour, yeast, and water.

ingredients.name: one peck or two gallons of fine wheat flour
ingredients.sourceText: one peck or two gallons of fine wheat flour

ingredients.name: half a pint of warm water
ingredients.sourceText: half a pint of warm water

ingredients.name: half a pint of strong fresh yeast
ingredients.sourceText: half a pint of strong fresh yeast

ingredients.name: three quarters to a whole pint home-made yeast

ingredients.name: three or four table-spoonfuls fine salt

steps: Sift flour into a kneading trough, or into a small clean tub, or a large broad earthen pan
Make a deep hole in the middle of the heap of flour
Have ready half a pint of warm water, which in summer should be only lukewarm, but even in winter it must not be hot or boiling
Stir water well into half a pint of strong fresh yeast
Pour it into the hole in the middle of the flour
With a spoon work in the flour round the edges of the liquid, so as to bring in by degrees sufficient flour to form a thin batter
Stir the batter well about for a minute or two
Take a handful of flour, and scatter it thinly over the top of this batter, so as to cover it entirely
Lay a warmed cloth over the whole, and set it to rise in a warm place
When the batter has risen so as to make cracks in the flour on the top, scatter over it three or four table-spoonfuls of fine salt
Begin to form the whole mass into a dough, commencing round the hole containing the batter, and pouring as much soft water as is necessary to make the flour mix with the batter
Knead it hard, turning it over, pressing it, folding it, and working it thoroughly with your clenched hands for twenty minutes or half an hour, till it becomes perfectly light and stiff
Form the dough into a lump in the middle of the trough or pan, and scatter a little dry flour thinly over it
Cover it, and set it again in a warm place to undergo a farther fermentation for about twenty minutes or half an hour
Heat the oven with faggots or small light wood
When the bread is ready, clear out the coals, and sweep and wipe the floor of the oven clean
Try the heat of the bottom by throwing in some flour
Put the dough on the paste-board, which must be sprinkled with flour
Divide it into loaves, forming them of a good shape
Place them in the oven, and close up the door
Bake for two hours and a half to three hours, or more, according to their size
When the loaves are done, wrap each in a clean coarse towel, and stand them up on end to cool slowly

title: Bread-and-Butter Pudding
description: A pudding made with bread, eggs, and milk.
steps: Cut thin slices of bread (stale), spread thickly with butter, and sprinkle with sugar
Fit them neatly and closely into a buttered pudding-dish until it is half full

Lay a small, heavy plate upon them to prevent them from floating, and saturate them gradually with a hot custard made of the milk, heated almost to boiling, then taken from the fire, and the beaten eggs and sugar stirred in with the seasoning
Let the bread soak in this fifteen minutes or so, adding by degrees all the custard
Just before you put the pudding in the oven, take up the plate gently
If the bread still rise to the top, keep down with a silver fork or spoon, laid upon it from the side of the dish, until the custard thickens, when slip it out
Eat cold

title: Broiled Chicken
description: Prepared with chicken, salt, and pepper.
steps: Dress for broiling, following directions on page 244.
Sprinkle with salt and pepper, and place in a well-greased broiler.
Broil twenty minutes over a clear fire, watching carefully and turning broiler so that all parts may be equally browned.

Remove to a hot platter, spread with soft butter, and sprinkle with salt and pepper.

description: Prepared with clams, potatoes, and clam.
steps: Clean and broil fish as directed in Ways of Cooking Fish.
When nearly cooked, slip from broiler onto a hot platter and brush over with melted butter.
Surround with two borders of mashed potatoes, one-inch apart, forced through a pastry bag and tube.
Arrange ten halves of clam-shells between potato borders, at equal distances.

Melt two tablespoons butter, add chopped clams, two tablespoons flour, and pour on gradually one-third cup cream.
Strain sauce, add soft part of clams, cook one minute, season with salt and cayenne, and add yolk of one egg slightly beaten.
Just before serving, fill clam-shells with Fricassee of Clams.

title: Calf's Brains Fritters
description: Prepared with brains, lemon juice, and onion.
steps: Clean brains, and cook twenty minutes in boiling water, to which is added one-half teaspoon salt, {{source-2}}, three cloves, two slices onion, and one-half bay leaf.

Add brains, and drop mixture by spoonfuls into greased muffin rings, placed in a frying-pan in which there is a generous supply of hot lard.
Cook on one side until well browned, turn, and cook other side.
Arrange on serving dish and pour around Sauce Finiste.

description: A soup made with calf's feet, lemon-peel, and water.

ingredients.name: the beaten yolk of an egg
ingredients.sourceText: the beaten yolk of an egg

steps: Boil two calf's feet in two quarts of water, till the liquid is reduced one half, and the meat has dropped to pieces.

When it has nearly boiled, stir in by degrees the beaten yolk of an egg, and then take it off immediately.
You may add to it a little sugar, and some grated lemon-peel and nutmeg.

title: Calf's Feet Fricassee
description: Prepared with calf's feet, gravy, and white wine.
steps: Boil the feet till very tender, cut them in two and pull out the large bones.
Have half a pint of good white gravy, add to it a spoonful of white wine, one of lemon pickle, and some salt, with a tea-spoonful of curry powder.
Stew the feet in it fifteen minutes, and thicken it with the yelks of two eggs, a gill of milk, a large spoonful of butter, and two of white flour.
Let the thickening be very smooth, shake the stew pan over the fire a few minutes, but do not let it boil lest the eggs and milk should curdle.

title: Calf's Head with Gravy and Forcemeat
description: A sauce made with gravy, forcemeat, and red wine.
steps: Boil pounded cloves, mace, salt, and cayenne pepper together till reduced to a pint, strain it, and add two gills of red wine, one of mushroom and one of walnut catsup.
Thicken it with butter and brown flour.
The head must be cut in small pieces and stewed a few minutes in the gravy.
Put a paste round the edge of a deep dish, three folds, one on the other, but none on the bottom.
Pour in the meat and gravy, and bake it till the paste is done.
Pick all strings from the brains, pound them, and add grated bread, pepper and salt.
Make them in little cakes with the yelk of an egg, fry them a nice brown.
Boil six egg's hard, leave one whole and divide the others exactly in two.
Have some bits of paste nicely baked.
When the head is taken from the oven, lay the whole egg in the middle, and dispose the others, with the brain cakes and bits of paste tastily around it.
If it be wanted as soup, do not reduce the gravy so much, and after stewing the head, serve it in a tureen with the brain cakes and forcemeat balls fried, in place of the eggs and paste.

The tongue should be salted and put in brine; they are very delicate, and four of them boiled and pealed, and served with four small chickens boiled, make a handsome dish, either cold or hot, with parsley and butter poured over them.

title: Calf's Liver and Bacon
description: Prepared with bacon, calf liver, and water.
steps: Slice the liver a quarter of an inch thick.
Pour hot water over it and let it remain for a few minutes to clear it from blood.
Dry it in a cloth.
Take a pound of bacon, or as much as you require, and cut the same number of thin slices as you have of liver.
Fry the bacon to a nice crisp.
Take it out and keep it hot.
Season the liver with pepper and salt and dredge in a little flour.
Lay it in the hot bacon fat and fry it a nice brown.
Serve it with a slice of bacon on the top of each slice of liver.
If you wish a gravy with it, pour off most of the fat from the frying pan.
Put in about two ounces of butter and a tablespoonful of flour well rubbed in.
Add a cup of water, salt and pepper.
Give it one boil and serve in a gravy boat.

title: Calf's-Head (Scalloped)
description: Prepared with butter, pepper, and salt.
steps: Clean the head, remove the brains, and set in a cool place.
Boil the head until the meat slips easily from the bones.
Take it out and chop fine, season with herbs, pepper, and salt.
Put in layers into a buttered pudding-dish with bits of butter between each layer.
Moisten well with the liquor in which the head was boiled.
Wash the brains very thoroughly, removing all the membrane.
Beat them into a smooth paste, season with pepper and salt, and stir in with them two eggs beaten very light.
Spread this evenly over the scallop, dredge the top with a little flour, and bake to a delicate brown.

Take out the calves' feet, and put them on a dish

Put the soup again into the pot, and give it a boil up
Toast two or three large thick slices of bread; cut it into small square dice or mouthfuls; lay it in the bottom of the tureen
Pour the soup over it, and put on the tureen cover immediately

title: Calves' Foot Jelly
description: Prepared with calves' feet, madeira, and brandy.

ingredients.name: a pound of broken up loaf-sugar per quart
ingredients.sourceText: a pound of broken up loaf-sugar per quart

ingredients.name: a pint of Madeira wine per quart
ingredients.sourceText: a pint of Madeira wine per quart

ingredients.name: a large glass of brandy per quart
ingredients.sourceText: a large glass of brandy per quart

ingredients.name: three large sticks of the best Ceylon cinnamon per quart
ingredients.sourceText: three large sticks of the best Ceylon cinnamon per quart

ingredients.name: grated peel and juice of four large lemons
ingredients.sourceText: grated peel and juice of four large lemons

steps: Boil a set of feet in four quarts of cold water (if the feet have been skinned allow but three quarts); they should boil slowly till the liquid is reduced to two quarts or one half the original quantity, and the meat has dropped in rags from the bone.
Strain the liquid; measure and set it away in a large earthen pan to get cold; and let it rest till next morning.
If you do not find it a firm cake of jelly, boil it over again with an ounce of isinglass, and again set it away till cold and congealed.
Remove the sediment from the bottom of the cake of jelly, and carefully scrape off all the fat.
Press some clean blotting paper all over it to absorb what little grease may yet remain.
Cut the cake of jelly into pieces, and put it into a porcelain kettle to melt over the fire.

To each quart allow a pound of broken up loaf-sugar, a pint of Madeira wine, and a large glass of brandy; three large sticks of the best Ceylon cinnamon broken up (if common cinnamon, use four sticks), the grated peel and juice of four large lemons; and lastly, the whites of four eggs strained, but not beaten.
Mix all the ingredients well together, and put them to the jelly in the kettle.
Set it on the fire, and boil it hard for twenty minutes, but do not stir it.
Throw in a tea-cup of cold water, and boil it five minutes longer.
Take the kettle off the fire, and set it aside, keeping it closely covered for half an hour.
Take a large white flannel jelly-bag; suspend it by the strings to a wooden frame made for such purposes, or to the legs of a table.
Pour in the mixture boiling hot, and when it is all in, close up the mouth of the bag that none of the flavour may evaporate.
Hang it over a deep white dish or bowl, and let it drip slowly, but on no account squeeze the bag.
If it is not clear the first time, empty the bag, wash it, put in the jelly that has dripped into the dish, and pass it through again.
Repeat this till it is clear.
Put it into moulds to congeal, setting them in a cold place.
When it is quite firm, wrap a cloth that has been dipped in hot water, round the moulds to make the jelly turn out easily.
